title: Sorting out problems
goal: Complain about a wrong or faulty order, ask for a refund or an exchange, report a lost phone or a scam to the police, retell exactly who said what, and calm an argument down.
intro:
Things go wrong: the shop sends the wrong colour, a new phone dies after a day, the warranty 'doesn't cover the screen', your phone stays behind in a taxi. Sorting it out in Pashto means being firm but calm — and being able to say exactly what everyone said: 'your colleague told me to bring it back', 'I asked him when it would come', 'he promised to fix it'.

This unit completes **reported speech**: statements, questions ('whether … or not'), and commands, requests and promises ('he told me to …', 'I asked him to …').

grammar.title: Reporting statements and questions
grammar.body:
Unit 20 showed the basic rule: Pashto reports speech after **چې** in the speaker's **original words**. Here is the whole system.

**1. Two styles for statements.** The usual spoken style keeps the original pronouns and tense: هغه وويل چې **زه** ستړی **يم** 'he said he was tired' (lit. he said: 'I am tired'). You will also hear the 'English' style, with the pronoun shifted: هغه وويل چې **هغه** ستړی **دی**. Both are fine; the first is more common in speech, the second avoids confusion when there are several people in the story. The tense never shifts: 'he said it **would** come' is وويل چې سبا **به** راشي (lit. 'it will come').

**2. The reporting verb.**
- **وويل** 'said' (a single statement). Past, so ergative: **ما / تا / هغه / هغې / هغوی** وويل, or a clitic: **راته يې وويل** 'he/she told me'.
- **ويل يې** (wayə́l ye) 'he was saying' — the imperfective past, extremely common when telling what happened: ويل يې چې … 'he goes …, he was like …'.
- **وايي چې** 'says', **ويلي يې دي** 'has said', **ويلي وو** 'had said'.

**3. Questions.** Keep the question word where it was: ما ترې وپوښتل چې **کله** به راشي 'I asked him when it would come'. **ترې** (tre) is 'from him / her / them' — in Pashto you ask something **from** someone (له X نه پوښتل); likewise **رانه** 'from me', **درنه** 'from you'. For yes/no questions add **که نه** 'or not' at the end — this is how Pashto says 'whether': وپوښتل چې پيسې مو ترلاسه کړې **که نه** 'he asked whether we'd got the money'.

**The trap:** the speaker of a past ويل or پوښتل is oblique — **ما** وويل, never زه وويل; **چا** وويل؟ 'who said?', never څوک وويل.

grammar.title: 'He told me to …': commands, requests and promises
grammar.body:
English turns a command into 'told me **to** …'. Pashto has two ways, both after **چې**:

**1. Keep the imperative** (the original words): راته يې وويل چې **صبر وکړه** 'he told me to wait' (lit. he said to me: 'wait!').

**2. Use the subjunctive** with the person who has to do it: راته يې وويل چې صبر **وکړم** 'he told me (that I should) wait', ورته مې وويل چې **راشي** 'I told him to come'. This is the safer choice when the imperative would be confusing.

**Negative:** imperative style **مه**: وويل يې چې **مه** ځه 'he told me not to go'; subjunctive style **ونه / نه**: چې **ونه** ځم.

**Asking someone to do something:** **له X نه غوښتل چې** + subjunctive: له مالک نه مې **وغوښتل** چې پيسې بېرته **راکړي** 'I asked the landlord to give the money back'. (پوښتل is for questions; غوښتل is for requests.)

**Promising:** **ژمنه کول چې** + به + verb: ژمنه يې وکړه چې سبا **به** يې جوړ **کړي** 'he promised to fix it tomorrow'.

**The trap:** after a command or request, the verb after چې is a **subjunctive or imperative**, never the plain present or past. راته يې وويل چې سبا **راځم** means 'he told me "I'm coming tomorrow"' — something completely different from چې سبا **راشه** / **راشم** 'he told me to come tomorrow'.

lines.en: (later, on the phone to her sister) The manager told me it was their mistake, and he gave me a charger as well!

culture:
In a shop, a calm, polite customer who knows what she's owed gets much further than one who shouts: **چيغې** make the other side lose face and dig in. Address staff as **ورور** 'brother' or **کاکا** 'uncle', and they will call you **خور جانې** 'sister' or **وروره** — it makes a dispute personal in a good way. Asking for **مسؤل سړی** 'the person in charge' is normal and not rude.

For anything stolen or lost you need a police report — in Afghanistan from the local **حوزه** (police district), in Pakistan from the **تهانه** — and in Pakistan the **15** helpline. Bigger disputes between families, neighbours or business partners are still often settled outside the courts by a **جرګه**: respected elders who listen to both sides and work out a **روغه** that lets everyone keep their honour. Between friends, a hurt feeling is a **ګيله**, not a شکايت — and **ګيله مې مه کوه** 'don't hold it against me' is how you start to make up.

tip.title: Firm but polite
tip.body:
- Ask for what you're owed plainly: **پيسې مې بېرته غواړم** 'I want my money back', **بدل يې کړئ** 'exchange it'.
- Back it up: **رسيد**, **ضمانت**, **دا زما حق دی**.
- Stay in the polite تاسو form (-əy) — it makes it hard for them to be rude back.

tip.title: He said … · I asked …
tip.body:
- **وويل چې** + the original words: وويل چې پارسل **به** سبا راشي.
- The speaker is oblique: **ما** / **هغې** وويل, **چا** وويل؟
- Ask *from* someone: ما **ترې** وپوښتل چې کله …
- 'Whether' = **… که نه** at the end.
tip.pattern: X وويل چې … · ما ترې وپوښتل چې … که نه

tip.title: 'Told me to …' = چې + imperative or subjunctive
tip.body:
- Keep the command: راته يې وويل چې فورمه ډکه **کړه**.
- Or the subjunctive: راته يې وويل چې سبا **راشم**.
- 'Not to': چې **مه** ځه. Ask someone to: له X نه مې **وغوښتل** چې …
- Promise: **ژمنه** يې وکړه چې … **به** …
tip.pattern: راته يې وويل چې + imperative / subjunctive
